# The standard library

<!-- Generated by `node docs/gen-std.ts` from std/*.tape and compiler/types.ts. Do not edit: edit the comments in std/ and run it again. `node docs/gen-std.ts --check` (in proof/all.ts) fails when this file is stale. -->

Every program is compiled with these files before its own, so everything here is in scope without an import. Arguments are named (`until(v: raw, byte: 10)`), but the first may go without its name (`until(raw, byte: 10)`), and an argument whose value is a name of the same name may be written bare (`until(v, byte)`). `a |> f(b: 1)` is `f(<first parameter>: a, b: 1)`. A program may define a function of the same name as one here; its own wins. For the language itself see [LANGUAGE.md](../LANGUAGE.md); for a whole service, [the guide](guide.md).

The examples under a function (`> expression`, then what it gives) are run by `tape test` on every commit. Each file also has helpers that these functions call: each is a `private fn`, which a program cannot call (C94; a function of its own of the same name is its own), and the types they pass among themselves (their comments start `Internal:`). They are in the source, std/*.tape, and not listed here.

## Common tasks

### Respond with JSON

`json(status: …, value: …)` answers a value as `application/json`. For a body written in steps, write it first and give it its type last: `buf() |> write_rows(rows: …) |> respond_as(status: 200, content: Json)`. `empty(status: …)` answers no body. An error is `problem(status: …, detail: …)`, application/problem+json (RFC 9457), the shape the service answers its own errors in.

```tape
type Item {
  Item(id: Int, name: View)
}

fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(method: Get, path: "/item") -> json(status: 200, value: Item(id: 1, name: "lamp"))
    _ -> problem(status: 404, detail: "no such item")
  }
}
```

Uses: [`json`](#fn-json), [`respond_as`](#fn-respond_as), [`Content`](#type-content), [`write_json`](#builtin-write_json), [`write_rows`](#fn-write_rows), [`empty`](#fn-empty), [`problem`](#fn-problem).

### Answer an error

`problem(status: 404, detail: "no such link")` answers `{"type":"about:blank","title":"Not Found","status":404,"detail":"no such link"}` as `application/problem+json` (RFC 9457): the title is the status's reason phrase, and `detail` says what went wrong with this request. The service answers its own errors in the same shape, so a client reads one. What a client needs to act on goes in members of the problem's own: `problem_with(status:, detail:, members: R)` writes the fields of the record `R` after `detail`. A status written as a literal outside 400 to 599 is C96.

```tape
type Conflict {
  Conflict(key: View, version: Int)
}

fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(method: Put, path: "/k/" ++ key) -> problem_with(status: 409, detail: "version mismatch", members: Conflict(key, version: 3))
    _ -> problem(status: 404, detail: "no such route")
  }
}
```

Uses: [`problem`](#fn-problem), [`problem_with`](#fn-problem_with), [`Content`](#type-content).

### Respond with an Atom feed

`buf() |> respond_as(status: 200, content: Atom)` answers `application/atom+xml` (the host adds `charset=utf-8`, which overrides an encoding declaration in the document). `Rss` is `application/rss+xml` and `Xml` is `application/xml`. Chrome renders these as pages; the service's content-security-policy is what stops a script in the document, and a host that serves them must send that policy.

```tape
fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(method: Get, path: "/feed.xml") -> buf() |> append(view: "<feed xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom'></feed>") |> respond_as(status: 200, content: Atom)
    _ -> empty(status: 404)
  }
}
```

Uses: [`respond_as`](#fn-respond_as), [`Content`](#type-content), [`respond`](#fn-respond).

### Read query parameters

`Request(query)` is the raw text after `?` (`None` when there is no `?`). A query string is encoded as a form is, so `form_field(body: query, name: "limit")` reads one parameter, decoded (`+` and `%XX`). The path never holds the query.

```tape
fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(method: Get, path: "/items", query) -> buf() |> append(view: "limit \(limit_of(query))") |> respond(status: 200)
    _ -> empty(status: 404)
  }
}

// ?limit=N, 1 to 100; 20 when it is absent or not a number
fn limit_of(query: Option[View]) -> Int {
  let Some(value: q) = query else -> 20
  match form_field(body: q, name: "limit") {
    Some(value: decimal(n)) if n >= 1 and n <= 100 -> n
    _ -> 20
  }
}
```

Uses: [`Request`](#type-request), [`form_field`](#fn-form_field), [`decimal`](#fn-decimal).

### Parse an integer, and route on one in the path

`decimal(v)` is `Some(n)` for canonical digits (no sign, no leading zero, at most 16 digits). Any function that returns an Option is a pattern, so `"/items/" ++ decimal(id)` routes and parses at once, and a refined type checks the range: `decimal(Id(id))`. `parse_int(text)` takes a number as people write one (a sign, leading zeros). `decimal_text(value)` and holes (`"\(n)"`) go the other way.

```tape
type Id = Int where self >= 1 and self <= 9007199254740991

fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(method: Get, path: "/items/" ++ decimal(Id(id))) -> buf() |> append(view: "item \(id)") |> respond(status: 200)
    Request(method: Get, path: "/items/" ++ _) -> buf() |> append(view: "bad id") |> respond(status: 400)
    _ -> empty(status: 404)
  }
}
```

Uses: [`decimal`](#fn-decimal), [`parse_int`](#fn-parse_int), [`decimal_text`](#fn-decimal_text).

### Decode a JSON body, with a 400 that says why

`decode(json: body, as: T)` is `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`, where `error` names the field and what is wrong: the `detail` of a 400 problem. Refined types validate while decoding; an `Option` field may be absent. Go on with `let Ok(…) = … else { … }`.

```tape
type Name = View where len(self) >= 1 and len(self) <= 80
type Qty = Int where self >= 1 and self <= 1000

type NewItem {
  NewItem(name: Name, qty: Qty, note: Option[View])
}

fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(method: Post, path: "/items", body) -> created(body)
    _ -> empty(status: 404)
  }
}

fn created(body: View) -> Response {
  let Ok(value: NewItem(name, qty)) = decode(json: body, as: NewItem) else {
    Err(error) -> problem(status: 400, detail: error)
  }
  buf() |> append(view: "\(qty) of \(name)") |> respond(status: 201)
}
```

Uses: [`decode`](#builtin-decode), [`Result`](#type-result), [`problem`](#fn-problem).

### Build a JSON list

`write_json` writes a `List` as an array, on its own or as a field, and `decode(json:, as: List[Item])` reads one back. For items computed from others, `map` them into a record type and write that. `write_rows(rows: sql_all(…))` writes the rows of a query as an array.

```tape
type Item {
  Item(name: View, qty: Int)
}

type Line {
  Line(name: View, double: Int)
}

fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(method: Post, body) -> counted(items: decode(json: body, as: List[Item]))
    _ -> json(status: 200, value: map(list: stock(), by: fn(i: Item) -> Line { Line(name: i.name, double: 2 * i.qty) }))
  }
}

fn counted(items: Result[List[Item], View]) -> Response {
  match items {
    Ok(value) -> buf() |> append(view: "\(length(list: value)) items") |> respond(status: 200)
    Err(error) -> buf() |> append(view: error) |> respond(status: 400)
  }
}

// A list is built with Cons and Nil, in a function that says its type (a `let` cannot tell which List a Nil is: C21).
fn stock() -> List[Item] {
  Cons(head: Item(name: "lamp", qty: 2), tail: Cons(head: Item(name: "desk", qty: 1), tail: Nil))
}
```

Uses: [`write_rows`](#fn-write_rows), [`write_json`](#builtin-write_json), [`List`](#type-list), [`map`](#fn-map).

### Money, exactly

Money is a `Dec[2]`: `12.30` is one, `price * qty` is exact, and a hole or `write_json` writes it with its two digits (JSON as text, `"12.30"`; decode takes a number or text, exactly). What loses a digit names its rounding, once: `mul` for a rate, `div` for a share. In the database a Dec is its count, an INTEGER (12.30 is 1230). A measurement is a Float instead (`1.5f`).

```tape
// three at the price in the query, with tax at 8.875% rounded once to the cent, half away from zero
fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  let Some(value: price) = parse_dec(text: query_of(raw), scale: 2) else -> empty(status: 400)
  let net = price * 3
  let tax = mul(a: net, by: 0.08875, scale: 2, rounding: HalfUp)
  let each = div(a: net + tax, by: 3, scale: 2, rounding: Down)
  buf() |> append(view: "\(net) + \(tax) = \(net + tax), \(each) each") |> respond(status: 200)
}

fn query_of(raw: View) -> View {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(query: Some(value: q)) -> q
    _ -> ""
  }
}
```

Uses: [`parse_dec`](#builtin-parse_dec), [`mul`](#builtin-mul), [`div`](#builtin-div), [`Rounding`](#type-rounding).

### Validate characters

`v[i]` is the byte at `i`, as an Int. `is_digit`, `is_lower`, `is_upper`, `is_alpha`, `is_alnum`, `is_space` and `is_hex` test one byte; `every_byte(v: …, keep: …)` is True when `keep` holds for every byte of `v`, and `keep` may be a function of your own.

```tape
// a slug: 1 to 32 bytes of a-z, 0-9 and -; decode's 400 for one that is not says the text after else
type Slug = View where len(self) >= 1 and len(self) <= 32 and every_byte(v: self, keep: slug_byte) else "1 to 32 of a-z, 0-9 and -"

fn slug_byte(b: Int) -> Bool {
  is_lower(b) or is_digit(b) or b == 45
}

fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  match request(raw) {
    Request(method: Get, path: "/s/" ++ Slug(s)) -> buf() |> append(view: s) |> respond(status: 200)
    _ -> empty(status: 400)
  }
}
```

Uses: [`every_byte`](#fn-every_byte), [`is_lower`](#fn-is_lower), [`is_digit`](#fn-is_digit), [`is_alpha`](#fn-is_alpha), [`is_alnum`](#fn-is_alnum), [`len`](#builtin-len).

### Advance to the next byte in a set

`scan(v:, at:, set:)` is the first position at or after `at` whose byte is one of `set`, a text literal, or `len(v)` when none is. It reads 16 bytes at a time and costs one step per 16 bytes read, rounded up. A CSV separator, the bytes HTML escapes and the bytes a line of Markdown stops on are sets of this form. `scan_plain(v:, at:)` is that scan for the bytes that end a JSON string's plain run.

```tape
fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  let at = scan(raw, at: 0, set: "*&<>")
  buf() |> append(view: slice(raw, from: 0, to: at)) |> respond(status: 200)
}
```

Uses: [`scan`](#builtin-scan), [`slice`](#builtin-slice), [`respond`](#fn-respond).

### Read a request header, set a response header

`header_of(request: r, name: "if-none-match")` is the header's value, `None` when it was not sent (the service passes accept, accept-language, content-type, if-match, if-none-match, if-modified-since, idempotency-key, user-agent, webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, webhook-signature and x-… (but not x-forwarded-… or x-real-ip), never cookie or authorization; and its own `tape-base`, the URL the program's `/` is at, without the last slash, for links and redirects to its other pages). `header(name:, value:)` adds one to an answer, before or after the body; the content type is `respond_as`'s.

```tape
fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  let r = request(raw)
  match r {
    Request(method: Get, path: "/old") -> empty(status: 301) |> header(name: "location", value: "/new")
    Request(method: Get, path: "/new") -> match header_of(request: r, name: "if-none-match") {
      Some(value: "v1") -> empty(status: 304)
      _ -> buf() |> append(view: "new") |> respond(status: 200) |> header(name: "etag", value: "v1")
    }
    _ -> empty(status: 404)
  }
}
```

Uses: [`header_of`](#fn-header_of), [`header`](#fn-header), [`Request`](#type-request).

### Check a signature

`hmac_sha256_verify(key:, data:, mac:)` is True when `mac` is the HMAC-SHA-256 of `data` under `key`, and compares every byte whatever they hold; `==` on two Views stops at the first byte that differs, which a caller can see in the time and the steps, so a signature is never checked with `==`. The mac arrives as text: `from_base64` reads it, or `from_base64url` for base64url without padding (each `None` for text that is not exactly an encoding). `sha256(data:)` and `hmac_sha256(key:, data:)` give 32 raw bytes; `hex`, `base64` and `base64url` write bytes as text. All are std code, metered in steps like any other (66 a 64-byte block). Standard Webhooks signs `id.timestamp.body` and sends `v1,<base64>`; the example signs the body alone.

```tape
fn handle(raw: View) -> Response {
  let r = request(raw)
  let Request(method: Post, path: "/hook", body) = r else -> empty(status: 404)
  let Some(value: sent) = header_of(request: r, name: "x-signature") else -> empty(status: 401)
  let Some(value: mac) = from_base64(text: sent) else -> empty(status: 401)
  match hmac_sha256_verify(key: signing_key(), data: body, mac) {
    True -> empty(status: 204)
    False -> empty(status: 401)
  }
}

// the key the sender signs with
fn signing_key() -> View {
  "a key shared with the sender"
}
```

Uses: [`hmac_sha256_verify`](#fn-hmac_sha256_verify), [`hmac_sha256`](#fn-hmac_sha256), [`from_base64`](#fn-from_base64), [`sha256`](#fn-sha256), [`hex`](#fn-hex), [`base64url`](#fn-base64url).

## Built-ins

Provided by the compiler itself. A built-in that needs a capability (`Sql`, `Remote`, `Clock`, `Entropy`, `Timer`) uses the one the entry point declares (`fn handle(raw: View, db: Sql, clock: Clock)`), by name, without passing it.

### builtin len

```tape
len(v: View) -> Int
```

The number of bytes in a View. (A Buf: `size`.)

### builtin slice

```tape
slice(v: View, from: Int, to: Int) -> View
```

The bytes from `from` up to, not including, `to`; no copy. `v[i]` is one byte, as an Int.

### builtin buf

```tape
buf() -> Buf
```

A new, empty buffer to write into: the body of an answer is written into one, then given its status with `respond`.

### builtin wrapping_add

```tape
wrapping_add(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
```

a + b modulo 2^64: the low 64 bits of the exact result. Plain `+` traps on overflow (trap 6); use this where wrapping is meant (a hash).

### builtin wrapping_sub

```tape
wrapping_sub(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
```

a - b modulo 2^64: the low 64 bits of the exact result. Plain `-` traps on overflow (trap 6); use this where wrapping is meant (a hash).

### builtin wrapping_mul

```tape
wrapping_mul(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int
```

a * b modulo 2^64: the low 64 bits of the exact result. Plain `*` traps on overflow (trap 6); use this where wrapping is meant (a hash).

### builtin float

```tape
float(n: Int) -> Float, float(n: Dec[s]) -> Float
```

The Float nearest `n`, a tie to the even one: exact up to 2^53 for an Int. The one way from an Int or a Dec to a Float; there is no implicit conversion.

### builtin dec

```tape
dec(n: Int, scale: s) -> Dec[s]
```

The Int as a Dec[s], exactly: `dec(n: 3, scale: 2)` is 3.00. Beyond the Decs it traps (integer overflow, trap 6). The scale is a number written in the call.

### builtin rescale

```tape
rescale(x: Dec[s], to: t) -> Dec[t]
```

The same number with more digits after the point, exactly (t ≥ s): `rescale(x: 1.5, to: 3)` is 1.500. Fewer digits is `round`. Traps (trap 6) when it does not fit.

### builtin round

```tape
round(x: Dec[s], to: t, rounding: Rounding) -> Dec[t]
```

The nearest Dec with fewer digits (t < s), as the rounding says: `round(x: 2.345, to: 2, rounding: HalfEven)` is 2.34.

### builtin to_int

```tape
to_int(x: Dec[s], rounding: Rounding) -> Int
```

The Int a Dec rounds to: `to_int(x: -2.5, rounding: HalfEven)` is -2, with `Floor` -3.

### builtin mul

```tape
mul(a: Dec[s], by: Dec[u], scale: t, rounding: Rounding) -> Dec[t]
```

The exact product, rounded once to t digits: `a * b` is a Dec[s + u], and this is for when that has more digits than you keep, or more than 18. The product is 128 bits, so it traps (trap 6) only when the result does not fit. `by` may be an Int.

### builtin div

```tape
div(a: Dec[s], by: Dec[u], scale: t, rounding: Rounding) -> Dec[t]
```

The quotient at t digits, rounded once: `div(a: 1.00, by: 3.00, scale: 2, rounding: HalfEven)` is 0.33. Exact in between (128 bits), so `a * b / c` loses nothing before the one rounding. By zero it traps (trap 4). `by` may be an Int. A Dec has no `/`.

### builtin parse_dec

```tape
parse_dec(text: View, scale: s) -> Option[Dec[s]]
```

The Dec[s] the text is, exactly: JSON's number syntax (`12.30`, `-0.5`, `1.23e1`), with no more digits after the point than s unless they are zeros (`12.300` is 12.30, `12.345` is None for a Dec[2]). No sign `+`, no spaces, no leading zeros.

### builtin write_dec

```tape
write_dec(out: Buf, value: Dec[s]) -> Buf
```

Appends a Dec with exactly its scale's digits after the point: `12.30`, `-0.05`, `0.00` (what a hole, `"\(x)"`, writes).

### builtin to_dec

```tape
to_dec(x: Float, scale: t, rounding: Rounding) -> Dec[t]
```

The Float's exact value (a binary fraction) rounded to t digits: `to_dec(x: 2.675f, scale: 2, rounding: HalfUp)` is 2.67, as 2.675f is a little below 2.675.

### builtin trunc

```tape
trunc(x: Float) -> Int
```

The Int toward zero: the one way from a Float to an Int (`floor` or `ceil` first for the other ways). Outside the Ints (beyond ±9.2e18) it traps, integer overflow (trap 6).

### builtin floor

```tape
floor(x: Float) -> Float
```

The integer below or equal, as a Float (`floor(-0.5f)` is -1).

### builtin ceil

```tape
ceil(x: Float) -> Float
```

The integer above or equal, as a Float.

### builtin sqrt

```tape
sqrt(x: Float) -> Float
```

The square root, correctly rounded; below 0 it traps (trap 8, float not finite).

### builtin sin

```tape
sin(x: Float) -> Float
```

The sine, x in radians. musl's, in Wasm: the same bits everywhere, within 1 ulp.

### builtin cos

```tape
cos(x: Float) -> Float
```

The cosine, x in radians. musl's, in Wasm: the same bits everywhere, within 1 ulp.

### builtin tan

```tape
tan(x: Float) -> Float
```

The tangent, x in radians; never infinite (no Float is that near an odd multiple of pi/2). musl's, in Wasm: the same bits everywhere, within 1 ulp.

### builtin asin

```tape
asin(x: Float) -> Float
```

The arcsine, from -pi/2 to pi/2; outside -1 to 1 it traps (trap 8, float not finite). musl's, in Wasm: the same bits everywhere, within 1 ulp.

### builtin acos

```tape
acos(x: Float) -> Float
```

The arccosine, from 0 to pi; outside -1 to 1 it traps (trap 8). `acos(x: -1f)` is `pi()`. musl's, in Wasm: the same bits everywhere, within 1 ulp.

### builtin exp

```tape
exp(x: Float) -> Float
```

e to the x; beyond about 709.78 it traps (trap 8, float not finite). musl's, in Wasm: the same bits everywhere, within 1 ulp.

### builtin log

```tape
log(x: Float) -> Float
```

The natural logarithm; of 0 or less it traps (trap 8). musl's, in Wasm: the same bits everywhere, within 1 ulp.

### builtin atan2

```tape
atan2(y: Float, x: Float) -> Float
```

The angle of the point (x, y), from -pi to pi; `atan2(y: t, x: 1f)` is the arctangent of t. musl's, in Wasm: within 1.5 ulp.

### builtin pow

```tape
pow(x: Float, y: Float) -> Float
```

x to the y. A negative x takes only an integer y, and a result beyond the largest Float traps (trap 8). musl's, in Wasm: within 1 ulp.

### builtin abs

```tape
abs(x: Int) -> Int, abs(x: Dec[s]) -> Dec[s], abs(x: Float) -> Float
```

The absolute value. Of the least Int (or Dec) it traps (integer overflow, trap 6).

### builtin min

```tape
min(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int, min(a: Dec[s], b: Dec[s]) -> Dec[s], min(a: Float, b: Float) -> Float
```

The smaller of two Ints, two Decs of one scale, or two Floats.

### builtin max

```tape
max(a: Int, b: Int) -> Int, max(a: Dec[s], b: Dec[s]) -> Dec[s], max(a: Float, b: Float) -> Float
```

The larger of two Ints, two Decs of one scale, or two Floats.

### builtin write_float

```tape
write_float(out: Buf, value: Float) -> Buf
```

Appends the shortest digits that read back as the Float: `0.1`, `1e+21`, `5` (what a hole, `"\(x)"`, writes). 128 steps: the host writes the digits (LANGUAGE.md section 10).

### builtin parse_float

```tape
parse_float(text: View) -> Option[Float]
```

The Float nearest the number `text` (`"0.1"`, `"-2.5e3"`), correctly rounded, the same everywhere; `None` when it is not finite (`"1e400"`) or `text` is not a number in the syntax of JSON, as `parse_dec` reads one (not `""`, white space, `+1`, `.5`, `5.`, `05`, `0x1F` or `Infinity`). decode reads a Float field with it. One step per 16 bytes of `text`, rounded up, and when it is not a plain decimal of at most 2^53 in its digits and 22 after the point, which the host reads, one a byte more and 64 for the call (LANGUAGE.md section 10).

### builtin scan_plain

```tape
scan_plain(v: View, at: Int) -> Int
```

The first position at or after `at` whose byte is below 32, 128 or more, a quote (34) or a backslash (92); `len(v)` when there is none. `scan(v:, at:, set:)` of those bytes, which a text literal cannot spell. Reads 16 bytes at a time (Wasm SIMD). One step per 16 bytes read, rounded up, as `scan(v:, at:, set:)` does. std/json.tape finds the plain runs of a string with it. `at` outside 0 to `len(v)` traps (trap 3).

### builtin scan

```tape
scan(v: View, at: Int, set: View) -> Int
```

The first position at or after `at` whose byte is one of `set`; `len(v)` when none is. `set` is a text literal: its bytes, escapes included (`\n` is byte 10), and a character's UTF-8 bytes are each members (`"é"` is bytes 195 and 169). The same byte twice is one member. Reads 16 bytes at a time (Wasm SIMD when the set has at most 16 bytes, or the JSON set of `scan_plain(v:, at:)`). One step per 16 bytes read, rounded up: every byte from `at` through the one it stops on, or from `at` to the end when it does not stop; `at` equal to `len(v)` reads nothing and costs nothing. `at` outside 0 to `len(v)` traps (trap 3).

### builtin push

```tape
push(buf: Buf, byte: Int) -> Buf
```

Appends one byte.

### builtin append

```tape
append(buf: Buf, view: View) -> Buf
```

Appends text. One step per 16 bytes appended, rounded up (LANGUAGE.md section 10).

### builtin freeze

```tape
freeze(buf: Buf) -> View
```

The bytes written so far, as a View.

### builtin size

```tape
size(buf: Buf) -> Int
```

The number of bytes written so far.

### builtin write_json

```tape
write_json(out: Buf, value: T) -> Buf
```

Appends a value as JSON, exactly the form `decode` reads back: a record as an object, its fields by name (`Int`, `Float` (the shortest digits that read back as it), `Bool`, `View` and refinements of them, records, `List[…]` of these, `Option[…]` of one); an `Option` field that is `None` has no key, and `Some(value)` is its value; a type with several constructors as `{"Constructor": {…}}` (`{"AlwaysUp": {}}` for one without fields); a `List` as an array; `Int`, `Bool`, `View` as themselves. Refused (C09): what cannot be JSON (a `Buf`, a function, `Option` inside a `List`).

### builtin decode

```tape
decode(json: View, as: T) -> Result[T, View]
```

Reads a JSON object into the record type `T`, or an array into `List[T]` (`as: List[Item]`). Of a type with several constructors it takes the one the object's only key names, `{"Sets": {…}}`, as `write_json` writes it; else the one that has all its fields among the keys and names the most of them. A key no field names is left unread: clients send more than a service reads. A missing key, a null, a wrong kind or a refinement that fails is `Err` with the path to it: `items[2].price: missing`, `key: null`, `qty: expected an integer`, `key: expected Key, 1 to 64 bytes`, `slug: not a valid Slug` (LANGUAGE.md section 6). An `Option` field that is absent or `null` is `None`. The bytes are read in the module, once (std/json.tape); a number is read exactly from its text.

### builtin next

```tape
next(rows: Rows[T]) -> Step[T]
```

One step through the rows of `sql_all`: `Next(value, rest)` or `End`. To go through all of them, `fold_rows`.

### builtin sql_first

```tape
sql_first(row: T, query: "… WHERE id = :id", id) -> Option[T]
```

Needs `Sql`. The first row the query returns, as `T` (its fields name the columns). Each `:name` in the query takes the argument of that name: `id` when a value of that name is at hand, `id: 7` otherwise. On a write it also takes `repeat: True`, for a write meant to apply again on each run: a count in SQL (`n = n + 1`) or an INSERT with no unique key (C54, C55; C88 refuses it where the write is safe without it); and `no_floor: True`, for a column it takes from that has no floor (C73).

### builtin sql_all

```tape
sql_all(row: T, query: "…", …) -> Rows[T]
```

Needs `Sql`. Every row, to fold with `fold_rows`, write as JSON with `write_rows`, or take one at a time with `next`. On a write it also takes `repeat: True`, for a write meant to apply again on each run: a count in SQL (`n = n + 1`) or an INSERT with no unique key (C54, C55; C88 refuses it where the write is safe without it); and `no_floor: True`, for a column it takes from that has no floor (C73).

### builtin sql_exec

```tape
sql_exec(query: "…", …) -> Int
```

Needs `Sql`. Runs a write; the number of rows it changed, which is read: `let 1 = sql_exec(…) else -> …` when the row must be there or the guard must hold, `let _ = sql_exec(…)` when the count does not matter. On a write it also takes `repeat: True`, for a write meant to apply again on each run: a count in SQL (`n = n + 1`) or an INSERT with no unique key (C54, C55; C88 refuses it where the write is safe without it); and `no_floor: True`, for a column it takes from that has no floor (C73).

### builtin sql_move

```tape
sql_move(row: T, query: "UPDATE … WHERE … RETURNING *", …) -> Move[T]
```

Needs `Sql`. A compare-and-set: `Moved(value)`, `Raced(now)` when the row was not in the state the WHERE names, `NoRow`. On a write it also takes `repeat: True`, for a write meant to apply again on each run: a count in SQL (`n = n + 1`) or an INSERT with no unique key (C54, C55; C88 refuses it where the write is safe without it); and `no_floor: True`, for a column it takes from that has no floor (C73).

### builtin call

```tape
call(to: Remote, method: "…", send: Msg, reply: Reply, error: E, within: Int, once: Key) -> Result[Reply, CallError[E]]
```

Needs `Remote`. A command to another program's `export fn`. The same `once` key runs at most once and gets the stored reply. `error:` names the callee's error type, which both programs declare: a refusal is `Err(error: Rejected(reason: …))`, a value of it, and a match names each constructor.

### builtin ask

```tape
ask(to: Remote, method: "…", send: Msg, reply: Reply, error: E, within: Int) -> Result[Reply, CallError[E]]
```

Needs `Remote`. A read from another program: `call` without a key.

### builtin remote

```tape
remote(of: Remotes, index: Int) -> Remote
```

Needs `Remotes`. One member of a family of Remotes: `remote(of: shards, index: fnv1a(v: key) % count)`.

### builtin now

```tape
now() -> Int
```

Needs `Clock`. Milliseconds since 1970, in the log so a replay sees it.

### builtin random

```tape
random() -> Int
```

Needs `Entropy`. 53 random bits, in the log.

### builtin secret

```tape
secret(name: View) -> Option[View]
```

Needs `Secrets`. The value of the program's secret of that name (the service's `PUT /_secrets/:account/:name/:secret`, the command line's `--secret name=value`), or None. The log records the name and the version read, never the value; a replay reads that version, and fails, saying so, when it is gone.

### builtin wake

```tape
wake(after: Int, key: Int) -> Done
```

Needs `Timer`. Asks the host to run the program's `export fn woken(…, message: Wake)` with `Wake(key)` after `after` ms. Setting a key again moves its time. Run it with `do wake(…)`.

### builtin rollback

```tape
rollback(out: Response) -> Response
```

Answers `out` and undoes this request's writes since its last call.

## std/core.tape

The types and functions the compiler itself refers to.

### type Option

```tape
type Option[T] {
  Some(value: T)
  None
}
```

A value that may be absent: Some(value) or None. `let Some(value: x) = e else -> fallback` goes on with x.

### type Move

```tape
type Move[T] {
  Moved(value: T)
  Raced(now: T)
  NoRow
}
```

What a compare-and-set did (sql_move). Moved: the row was in the state the statement compares, and is now as its RETURNING says. Raced: the row is there but was not in that state (another request moved it first); `now` is the row as it is. NoRow: there is no such row.

### type Result

```tape
type Result[T, E] {
  Ok(value: T)
  Err(error: E)
}
```

A value or the reason there is none. Errors are values: match on them, or go on with one case a step at a time, `let Ok(value: x) = e else { Err(error) -> … }`.

### type CallError

```tape
private type CallError[E] {
  Timeout
  Unreachable
  Rejected(reason: E) final
  Skew(reason: View) final
}
```

Why a call to another object or Worker gave no reply, with E the callee's refusal: `call(…, reply: Charged, error: ChargeError, …)` gives `Result[Charged, CallError[ChargeError]]`. Timeout: the time budget ran out, and for a call that changes something the outcome is unknown until it is sent again with the same key. Unreachable: nothing answers to that name. Rejected: it refused, and `reason` is the value of the callee's own error type, so `Err(error: Rejected(reason: Declined(why)))` is matched like any value, and a match names each constructor of E. Skew: the two sides disagree, so nothing ran this time: they were built from different definitions of the method (its message, its reply or its error: a constructor added to E on one side is a Skew, never a Rejected the other cannot read), the callee could not read the message, or the key was used before for another message (which may have run; do not compensate for a Skew as for a refusal); `reason` says which. Rejected and Skew are final: the callee runs a key at most once and repeats its stored reply, so the same call sent again gets the same answer; a timer that asks again does not change it (rules.ts C79 lets such an outcome leave a row for a request to move on). A capability the host binds (an `interface`) refuses with text: its E is View.

### type Done

```tape
type Done {
  Done
}
```

The value of a call run for what it does: wake gives it, and so does a function that only does something. `do f(…)` runs a call whose value is Done; a call with any other value is read (`let 1 = sql_exec(…) else -> …`), or dropped on purpose with `let _ = …`.

### type Wake

```tape
type Wake {
  Wake(key: Int)
}
```

What the host sends to `export fn woken` when a timer set with wake(timer, after, key) is due: that key.

### type Rounding

```tape
type Rounding {
  HalfEven
  HalfUp
  Down
  Up
  Floor
  Ceiling
}
```

How a Dec loses digits (round, to_int, mul, div, to_dec): HalfEven sends a tie to the even neighbour (2.5 to 2, -2.5 to -2), HalfUp sends it away from zero (2.5 to 3, -0.5 to -1); Down goes toward zero, Up away from it, Floor toward minus infinity and Ceiling toward plus infinity. The compiler reads the constructors in this order.

### fn value_or

```tape
fn value_or[T](given: Option[T], otherwise: T) -> T
```

The value an Option holds, or `otherwise` when it holds none. A refined type is its base type here: an `Option[Delay]` gives an Int where an Int is asked.

```
> value_or(given: Some(value: 3), otherwise: 0)
3
> value_or(given: None, otherwise: "none")
"none"
```

### type Step

```tape
type Step[T] {
  Next(value: T, rest: Rows[T])
  End
}
```

One step through the rows of a query: next(rows) gives Next(value, rest) or End.

### fn same

```tape
fn same(a: View, b: View) -> Bool
```

Text equality, used by == on View and by text patterns.

```
> same(a: "lamp", b: "lamp")
True
> "lamp" == "lamps"
False
```

### fn find_text

```tape
fn find_text(v: View, sep: View, at: Int) -> Int
```

Where sep first occurs in v, at or after at; -1 when it does not. Used by text patterns `p ++ "sep" ++ q`.

```
> find_text(v: "/runs/12/advance", sep: "/", at: 1)
5
> find_text(v: "abc", sep: "x", at: 0)
-1
```

### fn concat

```tape
fn concat(a: View, b: View) -> View
```

Text joined: `a ++ b` in an expression is concat(a, b). (In a pattern, `"prefix" ++ rest` takes text apart.)

```
> "Hello, " ++ "ada" ++ "!"
"Hello, ada!"
> concat(a: "", b: "")
""
```

## std/text.tape

Bytes and text.

### fn until

```tape
fn until(v: View, byte: Int) -> View
```

The part of v before the first `byte`, or all of v when it has none.

```
> until(v: "key=value", byte: '=')
"key"
> "no equals sign" |> until(byte: '=')
"no equals sign"
```

### fn after

```tape
fn after(v: View, byte: Int) -> View
```

The part of v after the first `byte`, or nothing when it has none.

```
> after(v: "key=value", byte: '=')
"value"
> after(v: "key", byte: '=')
""
```

### fn find

```tape
fn find(v: View, byte: Int, at: Int) -> Int
```

The position of the first `byte` at or after `at`, or len(v).


Does v begin with `prefix`?

```

True
> "/todo" |> starts_with(prefix: "/todos/")
False
```


Is `word` at position `at` of v?

### fn is_digit

```tape

```

Is the byte an ASCII digit, 0-9?

```
True
> is_digit(b: 'a')
False
```

### fn is_lower

```tape
fn is_lower(b: Int) -> Bool
```

Is the byte an ASCII lower-case letter, a-z?

```
> is_lower(b: "a"[0])
True
```

### fn is_upper

```tape
fn is_upper(b: Int) -> Bool
```

Is the byte an ASCII upper-case letter, A-Z?

```
> is_upper(b: "a"[0])
False
```

### fn is_alpha

```tape
fn is_alpha(b: Int) -> Bool
```

Is the byte an ASCII letter, a-z or A-Z?

```

False
```

### fn is_alnum

```tape
fn is_alnum(b: Int) -> Bool
```

Is the byte an ASCII letter or digit?

```
True
```

### fn is_space

```tape
fn is_space(b: Int) -> Bool
```

Is the byte white space: a space, a tab, a line feed or a carriage return?

```
True
```

### fn every_byte

```tape
fn every_byte(v: View, keep: Fn[Int, Bool]) -> Bool
```

Does every byte of v pass `keep`? True for "" (nothing fails). For a slug, a key or a code of a fixed alphabet:

```
> every_byte(v: "order-17", keep: fn(b: Int) -> Bool { is_lower(b) or is_digit(b) or b == '-' })
True
> every_byte(v: "Order 17", keep: is_alnum)
False
```

### fn char_count

```tape
fn char_count(v: View) -> Int
```

How many characters v holds: its code points, each UTF-8 sequence counted once, where `len` counts bytes ("é" is 2 bytes and 1 character). For a limit a spec states in characters: `type Name = View where char_count(v: self) <= 64`. Text that is not valid UTF-8 counts each byte that does not continue a sequence.

```
> char_count(v: "日本語")
3
> char_count(v: "é!")
2
```

### fn isqrt

```tape
fn isqrt(n: Int) -> Option[Int]
```

The square root of `n`, rounded down: the largest r with r * r <= n. None when n is negative. Exact for every Int, up to the largest (whose root is 3037000499). For fixed point, scale first: the root of 2 to 3 places is isqrt(2 * 1000 * 1000), 1414 thousandths.

```
> isqrt(n: 17)
Some(value: 4)
> isqrt(n: 2 * 1000 * 1000)
Some(value: 1414)
> isqrt(n: -1)
None
```

### fn digits_end

```tape
fn digits_end(v: View, at: Int) -> Int
```

The position of the first byte at or after `at` that is not a digit.

### fn decimal

```tape
fn decimal(v: View) -> Option[Int]
```

A canonical decimal number: digits only, no leading zero, at most 16 digits.

```
> decimal(v: "42")
Some(value: 42)
> decimal(v: "042")
None
> decimal(v: "12a")
None
```

### fn parse_int

```tape
fn parse_int(text: View) -> Option[Int]
```

An integer as people write one: an optional sign (`-` or `+`), then one or more digits, leading zeros and all; None for anything else, and for a number an Int cannot hold. For a value from a form, a query or a CSV field. `decimal` is the strict one, for ids in a path: no sign, no leading zero, so "/orders/007" is not order 7.

```
> parse_int(text: "007")
Some(value: 7)
> parse_int(text: "-42")
Some(value: -42)
> parse_int(text: "+5")
Some(value: 5)
> parse_int(text: "-9223372036854775808")
Some(value: -9223372036854775808)
> parse_int(text: "9223372036854775808")
None
> parse_int(text: "1.5")
None
> parse_int(text: "-")
None
```

```tape
fn decimal_text(value: Int) -> View
```

A number in decimal, as text.

```
> decimal_text(value: 2000)
"2000"
> "attempt " ++ decimal_text(value: -3)
"attempt -3"
```

### fn write_int

```tape
fn write_int(out: Buf, value: Int) -> Buf
```

Appends a number in decimal.

```
> buf() |> append(view: "n=") |> write_int(value: -305) |> freeze
"n=-305"
```

### fn write_text

```tape
fn write_text(out: Buf, text: View) -> Buf
```

Appends text: append(buf: out, view: text) with the names write_* use.

### fn write_code

```tape
fn write_code(out: Buf, code: Int) -> Buf
```

Appends a code point as UTF-8.

### type Utf8

```tape
type Utf8 {
  Utf8(code: Int, next: Int)
  BadUtf8
}
```

One UTF-8 sequence starting at a byte >= 128 (RFC 3629: no overlong forms, no surrogates, nothing above U+10FFFF).

### fn utf8_at

```tape
fn utf8_at(v: View, at: Int) -> Utf8
```

The code point that starts at `at` (a byte of 128 or more), and where the next one starts; BadUtf8 when it is not valid UTF-8.

### fn utf8_end

```tape
fn utf8_end(v: View, at: Int) -> Int
```

Where the UTF-8 sequence that starts at `at` (a byte of 128 or more) ends. When the bytes there are not UTF-8, it is negative: minus where their maximal part ends, the longest start of a sequence that is right so far (at least one byte), which a WHATWG decoder (TextDecoder) reads as one U+FFFD. So a loop that copies text and replaces what is not UTF-8 goes on at the end either way, as write_json_string does.

```
> utf8_end(v: "aé!", at: 1)
3
> utf8_end(v: buf() |> push(byte: 'a') |> push(byte: 195) |> push(byte: '!') |> freeze, at: 1)
-2
```

## std/json.tape

JSON (RFC 8259), read by stepping and written by appending.

Reading an object:   json_first(v) gives the first step, json_next(v, at) the step after a member:

```
Member(key, value, next)   one member; key is decoded; value is a Json; next is where to continue
Close(next)                the object ended at next
Malformed                  not JSON
```

Strings must be valid UTF-8 and well-formed Unicode: a lone surrogate escape is Malformed. A repeated key is reported again; the caller decides (JSON.parse keeps the last).

### type Json

```tape
type Json {
  JsonString(text: View)
  JsonBool(value: Bool)
  JsonOther
}
```

A value of a member, as json_first and json_next give it: text and booleans; anything else is JsonOther.

### type JsonStep

```tape
type JsonStep {
  Member(key: View, value: Json, next: Int)
  Close(next: Int)
  Malformed
}
```

One step through an object: a member, the end of the object, or text that is not JSON.

### fn json_first

```tape
fn json_first(v: View) -> JsonStep
```

The first step of the object that v holds (whitespace around it allowed).

### fn json_next

```tape
fn json_next(v: View, at: Int) -> JsonStep
```

The step after a member whose `next` was `at`.

### fn json_end

```tape
fn json_end(v: View, at: Int) -> Bool
```

Does only whitespace follow position `at`?

### fn json_value

```tape
fn json_value(v: View, at: Int) -> JsonValue
```

The value that starts at `at`.

### fn number_end

```tape
fn number_end(v: View, at: Int) -> Option[Int]
```

-? (0 | [1-9][0-9]*) (. [0-9]+)? ([eE] [+-]? [0-9]+)?

### fn skip

```tape
fn skip(v: View, at: Int, byte: Int) -> Int
```

at + 1 when v[at] is `byte`, else at.

### fn json_text

```tape
fn json_text(v: View, at: Int) -> JsonText
```

The string whose body starts at `at` (after the opening quote), decoded. A string without escapes is returned as a view of the input; one with escapes is decoded into new memory.

### fn is_hex

```tape
fn is_hex(b: Int) -> Bool
```

Is the byte a hex digit (0-9, a-f, A-F)?

```
> is_hex(b: 'F')
True
> is_hex(b: 'g')
False
```

### fn hex_value

```tape
fn hex_value(b: Int) -> Int
```

The value of a hex digit (is_hex(b) must hold).

```
> hex_value(b: 'f')
15
```

### fn is_json

```tape
fn is_json(text: View) -> Bool
```

Is text one JSON value (RFC 8259), with whitespace around it allowed? It accepts what decode accepts: strings are UTF-8, and a \u escape of a lone surrogate is allowed, as JSON.parse allows it. One pass over the bytes, with no tree built and no stack grown by nesting: on 64 KB of nested JSON, 99,358 steps and 8 bytes of memory (test/json-any.ts measures it on each build).

```
> is_json(text: " {\"a\": [1, -2.5e3, \"\\u00e9\"], \"b\": {\"c\": null}} ")
True
> is_json(text: "{\"a\": 1,}")
False
> is_json(text: "[1] [2]")
False
> is_json(text: "")
False
```

### fn json_member

```tape
fn json_member(json: View, key: View) -> Option[View]
```

The JSON text of the value of member `key` of the object that json holds, without the whitespace around it; None when json is not an object, has no member `key`, or is not JSON up to that member. Keys are compared once unescaped (`"\u0069d"` is `id`). Of two members with the same key the last is taken, as decode and JSON.parse take it, so a program that reads a body both ways reads one value; the whole object is read, and text after its closing brace is None, as decode refuses it. The value is read with decode: `decode(json: raw, as: View)` for a string, `as: Int` for a number, `as: T` for an object.

```
> json_member(json: "{\"id\": \"a1\", \"n\": [1, 2] }", key: "n")
Some(value: "[1, 2]")
> json_member(json: "{\"\\u0069d\": 7, \"id\": 8}", key: "id")
Some(value: "8")
> json_member(json: "{\"id\": 7} x", key: "id")
None
> json_member(json: "{\"id\": \"a1\"}", key: "name")
None
> json_member(json: "[{\"id\": 1}]", key: "id")
None
```

### fn write_json_string

```tape
fn write_json_string(out: Buf, text: View) -> Buf
```

Appends text as a JSON string, escaped exactly as JSON.stringify escapes it; bytes that are not UTF-8 are written as U+FFFD, one for each maximal part, as TextDecoder reads them, so what is written is always JSON.

```
> buf() |> write_json_string(text: "a\nb") |> freeze
"\"a\\nb\""
```

### fn write_bool

```tape
fn write_bool(out: Buf, value: Bool) -> Buf
```

Appends true or false.

```
> buf() |> write_bool(value: True) |> freeze
"true"
```

### fn json_int

```tape
fn json_int(text: View) -> Option[Int]
```

The value of a JSON number's text when it is a whole number within ±(2^53 - 1), read exactly (no rounding); None otherwise. `text` must be a JSON number (number_end found it).

```
> json_int(text: "1e3")
Some(value: 1000)
> json_int(text: "-2.50e1")
Some(value: -25)
> json_int(text: "1.5")
None
> json_int(text: "9007199254740992")
None
```

### fn write_rows

```tape
fn write_rows[T](out: Buf, rows: Rows[T]) -> Buf
```

Every row of a query as a JSON array, each row written as write_json writes it.

## std/http.tape

A request, parsed. The host passes METHOD SP TARGET LF BODY; the target is PATH or PATH?QUERY. A request that came through a published name's public route (no token: anyone) ends its line with a word, METHOD SP TARGET SP public, and `caller` is Anyone; one on the name's own origin with a session the host checked ends with ` session`, its id in the first header, the host's tape-session, and is Session(id); every other request is the operator's. The request headers the host passes follow on the same line, each after a carriage return, `CR name: value`, names in lower case. `query` is None when the target has no `?`, and Some("") when it ends with one: they are different requests. What `handle` gives back is a Response (below), never bytes: the host writes the status and the headers from it.

### type Caller

```tape
type Caller {
  Operator
  Anyone
  Session(id: View)
}
```

Who sent a request. Operator: it came with the operator's token. Anyone: it came through a published name's public route (`/p/:account/:name/…`, or the name's own origin) with no session. Session(id): it came on the name's own origin (`<name>--<account>.<PROGRAM_DOMAIN>`, docs/service.md#identity) with the cookie an answer of this program's `start_session(id:)` set there, which the host checked: signed with the service's key over this account, this name, the id and its expiry (30 days from its last use), so no other program's session, no expired one and no forged one is a Session. The id is what the program chose: Session says the client is the one this program started that session with, nothing about who that is beyond what the program knew when it started it. A Session request is public as Anyone's is: the program decides what it may do.

### type Method

```tape
type Method {
  Get
  Head
  Post
  Put
  Patch
  Delete
  Options
  Other(name: View)
}
```

The method of a request. A token HTTP does not name here (`PROPFIND`, a method in lower case: methods are case-sensitive) is Other with the token. The service runs a HEAD request as the GET it stands for and sends no body, so `handle` sees Get; Head is given only by a host that passes HEAD through.

### type Request

```tape
type Request {
  Request(
    method: Method,
    path: View,
    query: Option[View],
    body: View,
    caller: Caller,
    headers: View
  )
}
```

A request as `request(raw)` gives it. `path` is the target before `?`, as sent (percent-encoding is not undone); `query` the raw text after `?` (read one parameter with `form_field(body: q, name: "limit")`); `body` what follows the first line feed; `headers` the request headers the host passed, read with `header_of`.

```
match request(raw) {
  Request(method: Get, path: "/items/" ++ decimal(id)) -> …
  Request(method: Post, path: "/items", body) -> …
}
```

### fn request

```tape
fn request(raw: View) -> Request
```

The request `handle` is given, parsed.

```
> request(raw: "POST /holds?x=1 public\nqty=1")
Request(method: Post, path: "/holds", query: Some(value: "x=1"), body: "qty=1", caller: Anyone)
> request(raw: "GET /me session\rtape-session: ada\n")
Request(path: "/me", caller: Session(id: "ada"))
> request(raw: "PROPFIND /k\n").method
Other(name: "PROPFIND")
> request(raw: "GET /k/a b\n")
Request(path: "/k/a b", caller: Operator)
> request(raw: "GET /items?\n")
Request(path: "/items", query: Some(value: ""))
> request(raw: "GET /items\n")
Request(path: "/items", query: None)
> request(raw: "GET /k\raccept: text/html\n") |> header_of(name: "Accept")
Some(value: "text/html")
```

### fn header_of

```tape
fn header_of(request: Request, name: View) -> Option[View]
```

The value of a request header, by its name in any case; the first one when there are several. A host passes only the headers it means a program to see (the service's list is in docs/service.md: never cookie or authorization), and the service adds one of its own, tape-base: where the program is mounted.

```
> request(raw: "POST /\rcontent-type: text/csv\ridempotency-key: 7\nbody") |> header_of(name: "Idempotency-Key")
Some(value: "7")
> request(raw: "GET /\n") |> header_of(name: "accept")
None
> request(raw: "GET /\rx-a: 1\n") |> header_of(name: "accept")
None
```

### fn lower

```tape
fn lower(text: View) -> View
```

ASCII letters in lower case; every other byte as it is.

```
> lower(text: "Content-Type")
"content-type"
```

### type Content

```tape
type Content {
  Html
  Json
  Text
  Css
  Svg
  Csv
  Atom
  Rss
  Xml
  Problem
}
```

The content types the service serves: respond_as(body: b, status: 200, content: Html) answers text/html. Atom, Rss and Xml answer application/atom+xml, application/rss+xml and application/xml. The host labels those three, and the text types, charset=utf-8, which overrides an encoding declaration in the document. Chrome renders these as pages: a script in the XHTML namespace runs, and nosniff does not stop it. The service's content-security-policy does, and any host that serves these types must send that policy. application/xhtml+xml is not a Content: a page is Html. text/xml is not one: it is obsolete and was sniffed. Problem is application/problem+json (RFC 9457), what `problem` answers: an error a client reads as one shape.

### type Header

```tape
type Header {
  Header(name: View, value: View)
}
```

A response header, as `header` adds one: the name in lower case, and the value as given.

### type Response

```tape
type Response {
  Response(status: Int, content: Content, headers: List[Header], body: View)
}
```

What `handle` answers: a status, the type of the body, the headers set with `header` (the last one set first), and the body. The host writes the status line and the headers from these fields, so no byte of the body, from a request or a row, can become a status or a header. Build one with respond, respond_as, json, empty or redirect. The host refuses (answers 500, and says why) a status outside 200 to 599, a body on 204, 205 or 304, a header it sets itself, and a name or a value it would not send.

### fn respond

```tape
fn respond(body: Buf, status: Int) -> Response
```

The body written so far, answered as text/plain with a status: the body is written first, from `buf()`, and the status is attached last.

```
> buf() |> append(view: "ok") |> respond(status: 200)
Response(status: 200, content: Text, headers: Nil, body: "ok")
```

### fn respond_as

```tape
fn respond_as(body: Buf, status: Int, content: Content) -> Response
```

The body written so far, answered with a status and a content type: `buf() |> write_rows(rows: r) |> respond_as(status: 200, content: Json)` answers application/json, `content: Atom` a feed. A value as JSON is `json`, one call.

```
> buf() |> append(view: "<feed/>") |> respond_as(status: 200, content: Atom)
Response(status: 200, content: Atom, body: "<feed/>")
```

### fn json

```tape
fn json[T](status: Int, value: T) -> Response
```

A value as JSON, answered as application/json: `json(status: 201, value: order)` is `buf() |> write_json(value: order) |> respond_as(status: 201, content: Json)`.

```
> json(status: 201, value: Cons(head: 7, tail: Nil))
Response(status: 201, content: Json, body: "[7]")
```

### fn empty

```tape
fn empty(status: Int) -> Response
```

A response with no body: `empty(status: 204)` for a delete, `empty(status: 304)` for a fresh cache.

```
> empty(status: 204)
Response(status: 204, body: "")
```

### fn redirect

```tape
fn redirect(to: View) -> Response
```

A redirect to `to`, a path or a URL: 303 See Other with a location. 303 is the one a browser follows with a GET whatever the request was, which is what answering a form's POST with the page to go to means; 302 lets a client send the POST again. Another status is `empty(status: 308) |> header(name: "location", value: to)`.

```
> redirect(to: "/links/7")
Response(status: 303, headers: Cons(head: Header(name: "location", value: "/links/7"), tail: Nil))
```

### fn problem

```tape
fn problem(status: Int, detail: View) -> Response
```

An error, answered as application/problem+json (RFC 9457): `{"type":"about:blank","title":<the status's reason phrase>,"status":<status>,"detail":<detail>}`. The one shape for every error a program answers, and the one the service answers for its own (docs/service.md), so a client reads `detail` whichever said no. `detail` is for the person reading it (what went wrong with this request), the status says what kind of failure it is; a client that needs more to act on (a key, a version) is given members of its own with problem_with. A status written as a literal outside 400 to 599 is C96.

```
> problem(status: 404, detail: "no such link")
Response(status: 404, content: Problem, body: "{\"type\":\"about:blank\",\"title\":\"Not Found\",\"status\":404,\"detail\":\"no such link\"}")
> problem(status: 422, detail: "qty: expected an integer").body
"{\"type\":\"about:blank\",\"title\":\"Unprocessable Content\",\"status\":422,\"detail\":\"qty: expected an integer\"}"
```

### fn problem_with

```tape
fn problem_with[T](status: Int, detail: View, members: T) -> Response
```

An error with members of its own (RFC 9457's extension members): the fields of `members`, a record of one constructor, written after `detail` as write_json writes them (an Option that is None has no key). Name no field type, title, status or detail: those are the problem's own.

```
> problem_with(status: 409, detail: "taken", members: Header(name: "key", value: "a")).body
"{\"type\":\"about:blank\",\"title\":\"Conflict\",\"status\":409,\"detail\":\"taken\",\"name\":\"key\",\"value\":\"a\"}"
```

### fn start_session

```tape
fn start_session(out: Response, id: View) -> Response
```

The answer, and a session started with `id`, 1 to 256 bytes of printable ASCII (a user's id once a password or a mailed link checked out): on the program's own origin (docs/service.md#identity) the host sets a cookie the program never sees, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, signed with the service's key over this account, this name, the id and its expiry, and the client's requests are `Session(id)` for 30 days from their last use. Anywhere else (the operator's route, /p/, a host with no origins of the programs' own) the host sets nothing. It is a header of the host's own, `:session`, which no answer sends.

```
> redirect(to: "/") |> start_session(id: "ada")
Response(status: 303, headers: Cons(head: Header(name: ":session", value: "ada"), tail: Cons(head: Header(name: "location", value: "/"), tail: Nil)))
```

### fn end_session

```tape
fn end_session(out: Response) -> Response
```

The answer, and the client's session ended: on the program's own origin the host clears the cookie, and the next request is Anyone. A header of the host's own, `:session-end`.

```
> empty(status: 204) |> end_session()
Response(status: 204, headers: Cons(head: Header(name: ":session-end", value: ""), tail: Nil))
```

### fn header

```tape
fn header(out: Response, name: View, value: View) -> Response
```

A response header: `respond(body: b, status: 200) |> header(name: "cache-control", value: "no-store")`. The name is written in lower case. A name is 1 to 64 token characters (letters, digits, and !#$%&'*+-.^_`|~) and a value up to 4096 bytes of printable ASCII, spaces and tabs (no CR, LF, NUL, or byte past ASCII: percent-encode a URL); the host refuses any other (the request is answered 500, and says why), and those it sets itself (content-type, which is respond_as's, content-length, set-cookie, the security headers…), and more than 32. Adding one copies nothing: the body is not touched.

```
> empty(status: 302) |> header(name: "Location", value: "/links/7")
Response(status: 302, headers: Cons(head: Header(name: "location", value: "/links/7"), tail: Nil))
```

### fn content_type

```tape
fn content_type(content: Content) -> View
```

The media type a Content is served as. The host writes the Content-Type header from it.

```
> content_type(content: Json)
"application/json"
> content_type(content: Atom)
"application/atom+xml"
> content_type(content: Rss)
"application/rss+xml"
> content_type(content: Xml)
"application/xml"
> content_type(content: Problem)
"application/problem+json"
```

### fn form_field

```tape
fn form_field(body: View, name: View) -> Option[View]
```

One field of an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body (what an HTML form POSTs), decoded: `+` is a space and %XX a byte. None when the form has no such field; the first one when it has several. Finding the field is a `scan` of `&` and `=`, one step per 16 bytes read, plus a few steps per pair passed. Only the value found is decoded. `+` is a space only in a form or a query: in a path it is a `+`, and a path segment is decoded with `percent_decoded`, which leaves it one.

```
> form_field(body: "qty=2&buyer=ada+l%C3%B6", name: "buyer")
Some(value: "ada lö")
> form_field(body: "qty=2", name: "buyer")
None
> form_field(body: "x=1&done", name: "done")
Some(value: "")
```

### fn percent_decoded

```tape
fn percent_decoded(text: View) -> Option[View]
```

A path segment with its percent-encoding undone (RFC 3986): each %XX is the byte XX, hex in either case. Apply it to a segment the route has already bound, as a pattern: `path: "/users/" ++ percent_decoded(name) ++ "/tickets"`. `Request.path` stays as sent, so the route is matched on the encoded path: a `%2F` in a segment cannot become a `/` that moves the match, nor `%2e%2e` a `..`. What comes out may hold `/`, `..`, a space or a NUL, so check it (a refined type) before it names anything. None when a `%` is not followed by two hex digits, and when the bytes are not UTF-8 once decoded: where JavaScript's decodeURIComponent throws. A `+` stays a `+`: it is a space only in form encoding, which `form_field` decodes. Its cost is in steps (LANGUAGE.md section 10): a `scan` for `%`, one step per 16 bytes read, and two steps an escape; then a check that the result is UTF-8, one step per 16 bytes of ASCII and three a character past it. A 1,600-byte segment with no escape takes 200 steps; `%C3%B6` (ö) 100 times, 702 (test/percent.ts).

```
> percent_decoded(text: "ada%20l")
Some(value: "ada l")
> percent_decoded(text: "a+b%2Fc")
Some(value: "a+b/c")
> percent_decoded(text: "l%C3%B6")
Some(value: "lö")
> percent_decoded(text: "100%")
None
> percent_decoded(text: "%zz")
None
> percent_decoded(text: "%C3")
None
```

### fn write_html

```tape
fn write_html(out: Buf, text: View) -> Buf
```

Text into HTML, as text: & < > " and ' are written as entities, so a value from a request (a name, a note) cannot open a tag or end an attribute.

```
> freeze(buf: write_html(out: buf(), text: "<b>Tom & \"Jo\"</b>"))
"&lt;b&gt;Tom &amp; &quot;Jo&quot;&lt;/b&gt;"
```

### type HttpReply

```tape
type HttpReply {
  HttpReply(status: Int, headers: List[Header], body: View)
}
```

The answer to a request `fetch` made: its status, its headers in the order they came (names in lower case), and its body, byte for byte.

### fn fetch

```tape
fn fetch(to: Http, method: Method, url: View, headers: List[Header], body: View, within: Int, key: Option[View]) -> Result[HttpReply, CallError[View]]
```

An HTTP request to another service, through the program's `Http` capability, shaped like `call`: Ok with the reply whatever its status (a 404 or a 500 is an answer; a redirect is not followed, its 3xx is the reply), or Err(Timeout) when no reply came within `within` ms (the request may have been received), Err(Unreachable) when the host has no network for the program, and Err(Rejected(reason)) when the host would not send it: a host not on the program's list, a URL that is not https, a header it refuses, a body over 64 KB, a reply over 1 MB. A fetch is a commit point, as a call is: what the run wrote before it is committed when it goes out.

Every method but GET and HEAD carries `key: Some(…)`, sent as the Idempotency-Key header, so a request sent again after a Timeout is one the other side can tell is a repeat (C100: a POST written with `key: None` does not build; a method that is a value and a None key is refused by the host). A run replayed from its log is answered from the log: the request is not made again.

The log records the request with each secret the run read (`secret`) written `[secret <name>]` wherever it stands in the URL, a header's value or the body, and the reply with each such value kept out of the log: a key sent as `authorization: Bearer …` is never in a log, a trace or a span.

```
fetch(to: http, method: Post, url: "https://api.stripe.com/v1/refunds",
  headers: Cons(head: Header(name: "authorization", value: "Bearer " ++ key), tail: Nil),
  body: "charge=ch_1", within: 2000, key: Some(value: "refund-" ++ id))
```

### fn method_name

```tape
fn method_name(method: Method) -> View
```

A Method as its token.

```
> method_name(method: Delete)
"DELETE"
```

## std/list.tape

An immutable list. Adding to the front shares the rest; nothing is ever changed in place.

### type List

```tape
type List[T] {
  Cons(head: T, tail: List[T])
  Nil
}
```

An immutable list: Cons(head, tail) or Nil. Build one in a function that says its type, `fn items() -> List[Item]`.

### fn length

```tape
fn length[T](list: List[T]) -> Int
```

How many items.

```
> length(list: Cons(head: 1, tail: Cons(head: 2, tail: Nil)))
2
```

### fn reverse

```tape
fn reverse[T](list: List[T]) -> List[T]
```

The same items, last first.

```
> Cons(head: 1, tail: Cons(head: 2, tail: Nil)) |> reverse
Cons(head: 2, tail: Cons(head: 1, tail: Nil))
```

### fn map

```tape
fn map[A, B](list: List[A], by: Fn[A, B]) -> List[B]
```

A new list with `by` applied to every item.

```
> Cons(head: 1, tail: Cons(head: 2, tail: Nil)) |> map(by: fn(x: Int) -> Int { x * 10 })
Cons(head: 10, tail: Cons(head: 20, tail: Nil))
```

### fn filter

```tape
fn filter[A](list: List[A], keep: Fn[A, Bool]) -> List[A]
```

The items for which `keep` is True, in the same order.

```
> Cons(head: 1, tail: Cons(head: 2, tail: Cons(head: 3, tail: Nil))) |> filter(keep: fn(x: Int) -> Bool { x % 2 == 1 })
Cons(head: 1, tail: Cons(head: 3, tail: Nil))
```

### fn fold

```tape
fn fold[A, B](list: List[A], from: B, by: Fn2[B, A, B]) -> B
```

Combine the items left to right, starting from `from`: by(by(from, first), second) and so on. `from` may be a Buf, handed from item to item, to write each item into it.

```
> Cons(head: 3, tail: Cons(head: 4, tail: Nil)) |> fold(from: 100, by: fn(acc: Int, x: Int) -> Int { acc - x })
93
> Cons(head: 1, tail: Cons(head: 2, tail: Nil)) |> fold(from: buf(), by: fn(out: Buf, n: Int) -> Buf { out |> write_int(value: n * 10) }) |> freeze
"1020"
```

### fn range

```tape
fn range(from: Int, to: Int) -> List[Int]
```

The Ints from `from` up to `to`, not `to` itself: none when `to` is not above `from`. Folded, it is a counting loop: `fold(list: range(from:, to:), …)` never makes the list, and takes a step a number, as over a list of that length (compiler/fuse.ts).

```
> range(from: -1, to: 2)
Cons(head: -1, tail: Cons(head: 0, tail: Cons(head: 1, tail: Nil)))
> range(from: 1, to: 5) |> fold(from: 0, by: fn(acc: Int, n: Int) -> Int { acc + n })
10
```

### fn fold_rows

```tape
fn fold_rows[A, B](rows: Rows[A], from: B, by: Fn2[B, A, B]) -> B
```

Combine the rows of a query in their order, starting from `from`, as `fold` combines a list's items: one step a row and one more, and no list is made. `from` may be a Buf, handed from row to row, to write each row into it:

```
fn names(out: Buf) -> Buf uses db {
  sql_all(row: Item, query: "SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY id")
    |> fold_rows(from: out, by: fn(o: Buf, item: Item) -> Buf { o |> append(view: item.name) })
}
```

(An example in a comment runs without a database, so test/fold-rows.ts runs this one.) A list of the rows is a fold into Cons, then `reverse`. A function value cannot use a capability (C44): a row that needs a query, the clock or entropy of its own is read with `next`, in a function that calls itself.

### fn join

```tape
fn join(list: List[View], sep: View) -> View
```

The texts with `sep` between each two.

```
> join(list: Cons(head: "a", tail: Cons(head: "b", tail: Cons(head: "c", tail: Nil))), sep: ", ")
"a, b, c"
> join(list: Nil, sep: ", ")
""
```

## std/map.tape

An immutable map from text to any value, kept in key order (an AVL tree). `put` returns a new map that shares all but one path with the old one; the old map is unchanged. Walk it in order by matching on Node(left, key, value, right) and Empty.

### type Map

```tape
type Map[V] {
  Node(left: Map[V], key: View, value: V, right: Map[V], height: Int)
  Empty
}
```

A map from text keys to values of type V. Start from Empty; put and get.

### fn before

```tape
fn before(a: View, b: View) -> Bool
```

Does a sort before b, byte by byte?

### fn compare

```tape
fn compare(a: View, b: View) -> Int
```

Where a sorts against b, byte by byte: -1 before it, 0 the same text, 1 after it. A text sorts before every longer text it starts.

```
> compare(a: "desk", b: "lamp")
-1
> compare(a: "lamp", b: "lam")
1
> compare(a: "rug", b: "rug")
0
```

### fn get

```tape
fn get[V](map: Map[V], key: View) -> Option[V]
```

The value under `key`, if there is one. One comparison of the keys at each node.

```
> Empty |> put(key: "lamp", value: 3) |> put(key: "desk", value: 1) |> get(key: "lamp")
Some(value: 3)
> Empty |> put(key: "lamp", value: 3) |> get(key: "rug")
None
```

### fn put

```tape
fn put[V](map: Map[V], key: View, value: V) -> Map[V]
```

A map with `key` set to `value`; the old map is unchanged. Setting a key again replaces its value. One comparison of the keys at each node.

```
> Empty |> put(key: "a", value: 1) |> put(key: "a", value: 2) |> get(key: "a")
Some(value: 2)
```

### fn put_with

```tape
fn put_with[V](map: Map[V], key: View, from: V, by: Fn[V, V]) -> Map[V]
```

A map with the value under `key` replaced by `by` of it, or set to `by(from)` when the key is not there: one walk down the tree where get and then put take two, and a path whose heights did not change is not balanced again. Counting words is `put_with(map: counts, key: word, from: 0, by: plus_one)`.

```
> Empty |> put_with(key: "a", from: 0, by: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n + 1 }) |> put_with(key: "a", from: 0, by: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n + 1 }) |> get(key: "a")
Some(value: 2)
> Empty |> put_with(key: "a", from: 10, by: fn(n: Int) -> Int { n * 2 }) |> get(key: "a")
Some(value: 20)
```

### fn count

```tape
fn count[V](map: Map[V]) -> Int
```

How many keys.

```
> Empty |> put(key: "a", value: 1) |> put(key: "b", value: 2) |> put(key: "a", value: 3) |> count
2
```

## std/retry.tape

When to try again, as a library on top of one capability. backoff is pure arithmetic; retry_later also sets a timer (wake, which needs Timer), so the host calls the program's `woken` with Wake(key) when the time comes. Nothing here is syntax, and a program that never calls it sets no timers.

### type Backoff

```tape
type Backoff {
  Backoff(first: Int, factor: Int, most: Int, tries: Int)
}
```

How long to wait after each failure in a row: `first` ms after the first, `factor` times longer after each one after that, never longer than `most` ms; and how many attempts in all, the first one included.

### type Retry

```tape
type Retry {
  RetryIn(after: Int, attempt: Int)
  GaveUp(tries: Int) final
}
```

What to do after a failure: try again in `after` ms (that will be attempt number `attempt`), or stop, because all `tries` attempts have failed. GaveUp is final: backoff gives it again for as many failures or more, so a row a program gives up on waits for a request (C79).

### fn backoff

```tape
fn backoff(policy: Backoff, failed: Int) -> Retry
```

After `failed` failures in a row (1 after the first), what to do. The same answer every time.

```
> backoff(policy: Backoff(first: 1000, factor: 2, most: 30000, tries: 5), failed: 1)
RetryIn(after: 1000, attempt: 2)
> backoff(policy: Backoff(first: 1000, factor: 2, most: 30000, tries: 5), failed: 3)
RetryIn(after: 4000, attempt: 4)
> backoff(policy: Backoff(first: 1000, factor: 3, most: 5000, tries: 9), failed: 4)
RetryIn(after: 5000, attempt: 5)
> backoff(policy: Backoff(first: 1000, factor: 2, most: 30000, tries: 5), failed: 5)
GaveUp(tries: 5)
```

### fn grown

```tape
fn grown(wait: Int, factor: Int, most: Int, times: Int) -> Int
```

`wait`, `times` times multiplied by `factor`, stopping once it reaches `most`.

```
> grown(wait: 10, factor: 2, most: 1000, times: 3)
80
```

### fn capped

```tape
fn capped(wait: Int, most: Int) -> Int
```

The smaller of the two: a wait never longer than `most`.

```
> capped(wait: 7000, most: 5000)
5000
```

### fn retry_later

```tape
fn retry_later(timer: Timer, key: Int, policy: Backoff, failed: Int) -> Retry
```

backoff, and when it says to try again, a timer for then: `woken` gets Wake(key) that many ms from now. The key names what to retry (an order's id, say); setting it again moves its time, so a key is retried once.

## std/time.tape

An instant, milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z as `now()` gives it, as a date and a time of day in UTC. Each function takes the instant as an argument and needs no capability: the clock is read once, with `now()`, and what is shown of it is computed. The calendar is the proleptic Gregorian one, with no leap seconds (a day is 86,400,000 ms), as JavaScript's Date and Unix time count. Every Int is an instant, before 1970 too: the days are counted by Howard Hinnant's civil_from_days, a few operations and no loop over the years.

### type Civil

```tape
type Civil {
  Civil(year: Int, month: Int, day: Int, hour: Int, minute: Int, second: Int, millisecond: Int)
}
```

An instant in UTC, by its parts: `month` 1 to 12, `day` 1 to 31, `hour` 0 to 23, `minute` and `second` 0 to 59, `millisecond` 0 to 999. `year` is astronomical: the year before 1 is 0, and before that -1.

### fn civil

```tape
fn civil(ms: Int) -> Civil
```

The date and time of day in UTC of an instant, milliseconds since 1970. For every Int: an instant before 1970 is negative, and its parts count forward from the start of its day as any other's (-1 is 1969-12-31 at 23:59:59.999); the least Int is in the year -292275055 and the largest in 292278994. It loops over nothing, so it costs no steps.

```
> civil(ms: 0)
Civil(year: 1970, month: 1, day: 1, hour: 0, minute: 0, second: 0, millisecond: 0)
> civil(ms: 1795615387123)
Civil(year: 2026, month: 11, day: 25, hour: 14, minute: 3, second: 7, millisecond: 123)
> civil(ms: 951782400000)
Civil(year: 2000, month: 2, day: 29, hour: 0)
> civil(ms: -1)
Civil(year: 1969, month: 12, day: 31, hour: 23, minute: 59, second: 59, millisecond: 999)
> civil(ms: -62198755200000).year
-1
```

### fn rfc3339

```tape
fn rfc3339(ms: Int) -> View
```

An instant as RFC 3339 text in UTC, `2026-11-25T14:03:07.123Z`: always the three digits of its milliseconds and `Z`, so every one is 24 bytes from 0000 to 9999 and they sort as text in the order of time. For JSON, Atom feeds and logs. RFC 3339 has years 0000 to 9999 only, from -62167219200000 to 253402300799999; outside them the year is ISO 8601's expanded one, a sign and at least six digits (`+010000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`), as JavaScript's toISOString writes it. Its steps are its numbers' digits, one each as decimal_text writes them: 20 for 2026.

```
> rfc3339(ms: 1795615387123)
"2026-11-25T14:03:07.123Z"
> rfc3339(ms: 0)
"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"
> rfc3339(ms: -1)
"1969-12-31T23:59:59.999Z"
> rfc3339(ms: 253402300800000)
"+010000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"
> rfc3339(ms: -62198755200000)
"-000001-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"
```

### fn http_date

```tape
fn http_date(ms: Int) -> View
```

An instant as an HTTP date (RFC 9110 section 5.6.7, IMF-fixdate), `Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:03:07 GMT`: for the date, last-modified, expires and retry-after headers. The milliseconds are dropped: the second it falls in. The same text as JavaScript's toUTCString. An HTTP date has years 0000 to 9999 only; outside them the year is written as toUTCString writes it, its digits after a `-` for a year before 0 (`-0001`), and a header should not be sent with one. Its steps are its numbers' digits, one each as decimal_text writes them: 16 for 2026.

```
> http_date(ms: 1795615387123)
"Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:03:07 GMT"
> http_date(ms: 784111777000)
"Sun, 06 Nov 1994 08:49:37 GMT"
> http_date(ms: -1)
"Wed, 31 Dec 1969 23:59:59 GMT"
```

## std/math.tape

Float's constants. Its functions (sqrt, sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan2, exp, log, pow) and its operators (+ - * / %) are built in, compiled into the module so they give the same bits everywhere: docs/std.md lists them with the built-ins.

### fn pi

```tape
fn pi() -> Float
```

pi, as the Float nearest it (0x400921FB54442D18, which JavaScript's Math.PI is). A function, as std has no constants: `deg * pi() / 180f` is radians.

```
> pi()
3.141592653589793f
> acos(x: -1f) == pi()
True
> 2f * asin(x: 1f) == pi()
True
```

## std/crypto.tape

SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4), HMAC-SHA-256 (RFC 2104) and the encodings that carry their bytes: hex and base64 (RFC 4648). They are written in Tape, so they need no capability, give the same bytes on every host and in a replay, and cost steps as any other code does (LANGUAGE.md section 10).

A digest is 32 raw bytes. SHA-256 works on 32-bit words; an Int holds 64 bits, so each word is kept from 0 to 2^32 - 1: a sum is taken back to 32 bits with `& 4294967295`, which is 2^32 - 1, and a rotation is two shifts of a value that is never negative.

### fn sha256

```tape
fn sha256(data: View) -> View
```

The SHA-256 digest of `data`: 32 bytes. Its cost is 66 steps for each 64-byte block hashed, and 1 more: the data with its padding (a 128 byte, zeros and its length in bits, 9 bytes at least) is a whole number of blocks, so 0 to 55 bytes are one block, 56 to 119 two, and n bytes (n + 72) / 64 blocks. It makes no copy of `data`.

```
> hex(bytes: sha256(data: ""))
"e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855"
> hex(bytes: sha256(data: "abc"))
"ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad"
> len(sha256(data: "abc"))
32
```

### fn hmac_sha256

```tape
fn hmac_sha256(key: View, data: View) -> View
```

The HMAC-SHA-256 of `data` under `key` (RFC 2104): 32 bytes. A key longer than the 64-byte block is hashed first, as the RFC says. Its cost is 65 steps for each of the two padded keys, the steps of its two digests, of 64 + len(data) bytes and then of 96 (133 steps), and its copies of the data and of the inner digest, a step per 16 bytes: 398 steps and one per 16 bytes of data for up to 55 bytes, and 66 more for each further 64 bytes; a key longer than 64 bytes adds the steps of its own digest. It copies the data once.

```
> hex(bytes: hmac_sha256(key: "Jefe", data: "what do ya want for nothing?"))
"5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843"
```

### fn hmac_sha256_verify

```tape
fn hmac_sha256_verify(key: View, data: View, mac: View) -> Bool
```

Is `mac` the HMAC-SHA-256 of `data` under `key`? Check a signature with this, not with `==`: `==` on two Views stops at the first byte that differs, so how long it takes, and how many steps a request takes when the check is written as a loop that stops, tells a caller how many leading bytes of a forged mac were right. This walks all 32 bytes whatever they hold and takes the OR of their XORs, so its steps and its time are the same wherever the bytes differ: hmac_sha256's steps and 33 more. A mac that is not 32 bytes long is False before any byte is compared (its length is not a secret).

```
> hmac_sha256_verify(key: "k", data: "body", mac: hmac_sha256(key: "k", data: "body"))
True
> hmac_sha256_verify(key: "k", data: "body", mac: hmac_sha256(key: "K", data: "body"))
False
> hmac_sha256_verify(key: "k", data: "body", mac: "")
False
```

### fn hex

```tape
fn hex(bytes: View) -> View
```

The bytes in lower-case hex, two digits a byte. One step a byte, and 1.

```
> hex(bytes: "Tape")
"54617065"
> hex(bytes: sha256(data: "")) |> slice(from: 0, to: 8)
"e3b0c442"
```

### fn base64

```tape
fn base64(bytes: View) -> View
```

The bytes in base64 (RFC 4648 section 4): A-Z, a-z, 0-9, + and /, padded with = to a multiple of 4. One step for each 3 bytes, and 1.

```
> base64(bytes: "hello")
"aGVsbG8="
> base64(bytes: ">>?")
"Pj4/"
> base64(bytes: "")
""
```

### fn base64url

```tape
fn base64url(bytes: View) -> View
```

The bytes in base64url (RFC 4648 section 5): - and _ where base64 has + and /, and no padding, as JWT and Standard Webhooks' signatures write it (so it can stand in a URL or a header unescaped). One step for each 3 bytes, and 1.

```
> base64url(bytes: "hello")
"aGVsbG8"
> base64url(bytes: ">>?")
"Pj4_"
```

### fn from_base64

```tape
fn from_base64(text: View) -> Option[View]
```

The bytes that base64 text stands for, or None. It takes exactly what `base64` writes and nothing else: None for a byte outside A-Z, a-z, 0-9, + and / (a space, a line break, base64url's - or _, an = that is not padding), for a length that is not a multiple of 4, and for a last character whose bits past the data are not zero ("aGVsbG9=" is not canonical: base64 of "hello" is "aGVsbG8="), so each value has one encoding. One step a character and one for each 4 characters, and 2.

```
> from_base64(text: "aGVsbG8=")
Some(value: "hello")
> from_base64(text: "aGVsbG8")
None
> from_base64(text: "aGVsbG9=")
None
> from_base64(text: "aGVs bG8=")
None
```

### fn from_base64url

```tape
fn from_base64url(text: View) -> Option[View]
```

The bytes that base64url text stands for, or None. It takes exactly what `base64url` writes: None for a byte outside A-Z, a-z, 0-9, - and _ (base64's + or /, and = too: base64url here has no padding), for a length that leaves 1 character over a multiple of 4 (no bytes give that), and for a last character whose bits past the data are not zero. One step a character and one for each 4 characters, and 2.

```
> from_base64url(text: "aGVsbG8")
Some(value: "hello")
> from_base64url(text: "Pj4_")
Some(value: ">>?")
> from_base64url(text: "aGVsbG8=")
None
> from_base64url(text: "Pj4/")
None
```
